content: Strep throat, also referred to as streptococcal pharyngitis or streptococcal sore throat, is a type of Group A streptococcal infection that primarily affects the pharynx. In the 4th century BC, Hippocrates described the cause of a scarlet fever epidemic as being related to Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, or GAS). In 1874, Billroth was the first to describe streptococcal infections. In 1919, Brown identified the blood agar hemolysis patterns of streptococci. Rebecca Lancefield, in the 1930s, classified beta-hemolytic streptococci into distinct serogroups. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis is most commonly transmitted through direct person-to-person contact, typically via saliva or nasal secretions from an infected individual. Rarely, outbreaks can occur due to contaminated food, particularly milk and milk products. The incubation period for Group A strep pharyngitis is approximately 2 to 5 days. The pathogenesis involves bacterial adhesion to the pharyngeal mucosa via surface adhesins, followed by invasion of mucosal tissue through the production of proteases and cytolysins, leading to inflammation and the clinical signs and symptoms of pharyngitis. The M protein on the surface of Group A streptococci plays a critical role in the development of rheumatic fever. Strep throat is caused by beta-hemolytic Group A streptococcal infection. The human skin and mucous membranes are the only known reservoirs for this bacterium. Over 80 serotypes of Group A streptococci have been identified based on the M protein. Certain serotypes, such as M types 1, 3, 5, 6, 14, 18, 19, and 24, are associated with GAS strep throat. These bacteria are approximately 2 µm in size, catalase-negative, facultative anaerobes or obligate anaerobes, encapsulated with a hyaluronic acid capsule, and require enriched media like blood agar for growth. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis worldwide, with an estimated annual incidence of over 616 million cases. It predominantly affects children aged 5 to 15 years and is rare in children under 3 years of age. The condition is more common during the winter and early spring seasons. Risk factors for developing strep throat include younger age (5–15 years), close contact with individuals infected with streptococcal pharyngitis, and overcrowded environments. There are no specific screening guidelines for strep throat. If left untreated, Group A streptococcal pharyngitis may resolve on its own. However, complications such as peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, mastoiditis, and cervical lymphadenitis can occur. Less commonly, delayed complications such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever, and toxic shock syndrome may develop. Rarely, vasculitis may occur. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis for strep throat is excellent, and complications are rare. The hallmark symptom of strep throat is the sudden onset of a sore throat. A history of contact with individuals with strep throat or being in overcrowded settings (e.g., schools, military recruits) may suggest Group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Common symptoms include high-grade fever, difficulty swallowing, headache, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, red and enlarged tonsils, red and black patches in the throat, halitosis, rash, frequent cold chills, and the absence of cough. On physical examination, findings may include fever (≥101°F), pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar erythema, tonsillar hypertrophy with or without exudates, palatal petechiae, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, an inflamed uvula, and a scarlatiniform rash. If viral symptoms (e.g., cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, oral ulcers, conjunctivitis) are present, testing for Group A strep is not necessary. However, clinical examination alone cannot reliably differentiate between viral and Group A strep pharyngitis in the absence of viral symptoms, even for experienced clinicians. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis can be diagnosed using a rapid antigen detection test (RADT) and throat culture. Throat culture is considered the gold standard diagnostic test. Individuals with a negative RADT but high clinical suspicion for strep throat should have their diagnosis confirmed with a throat culture. RADTs have higher specificity but lower sensitivity compared to throat cultures. A lateral neck X-ray may be used to diagnose complications of strep throat, such as retropharyngeal abscess, by showing widening of the prevertebral space. Echocardiography may be useful in diagnosing rheumatic fever carditis, a complication of strep throat, and in monitoring the progression of valve defects associated with rheumatic fever. There are no other diagnostic studies specifically for strep throat. The primary treatment for strep throat is antibiotic therapy, which helps reduce symptoms, minimize transmission, and lower the risk of complications. Surgery is not indicated for the treatment of strep throat. There are no vaccines currently available to prevent Group A streptococcal infections. Preventive measures include practicing good hygiene, such as frequent handwashing, covering coughs or sneezes, and staying home from work, school, or daycare until afebrile and at least 24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotic therapy.
